title: The summit
hookLine: five years of mornings; the Buddha said he only shows the way, and you walked it
tomorrow: the summit's behind you. so where does the path go from here?

cards: A map app can show the whole route, every turn glowing blue. It has never walked anyone home. A brahmin accountant named Moggallana put that problem to the Buddha.
You teach the path step by step, he said. Nibbana exists, the path exists, you're the guide. So does everyone you teach get there?
Some do, the Buddha said. Some don't. Then why, asked the accountant, when everything's laid out?
Five years of mornings end with his answer.

teach.b: The Buddha answered with a question. You know the road to Rajagaha? Someone asks you the way, and you tell them exactly: follow this road, you'll see a village, then a town, then the city and its parks.
One follows it and arrives. One takes the wrong road. What can you do?
You're one who shows the way.
So it is with me, the Buddha said: the Tathagata shows the way. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers."
That's the teaching at the top. The Buddha is a guide, not a ride; the walking belongs to the walker. A neighbor's book, from China, has its own step.
In the Tao Te Ching, as James Legge translated it, Laozi writes that "the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step." Both picture a long way crossed one step at a time.
Where they part: for Laozi the Tao is the nameless way of heaven and earth, followed by not forcing; for the Buddha the path is a road a teacher points out, to the end of dukkha.
Look back down the slope: the four truths, the immeasurables, the good given away, the path ahead, the night under the tree.

how: Buddhists honor the Buddha as the one who showed the way, and Dhammapada 276 is one of the verses that says so: teachers and the sangha guide, but the practice is one's own.

o: a mountain shrine where the Buddha's relics are kept
the top after five years: he showed the way, you walked it
the final vow a monk takes before teaching others

games.q: the view from the top — tap the pairs.
p: directions given; walking is up to you
a thousand li begins with one step

s: the Moggallana in this sutta is the Buddha's well-known chief disciple
he's a brahmin accountant, Ganaka Moggallana; the chief disciple only shares the name.
the Dhammapada calls the Tathagatas only preachers
in Max Müller's translation: you yourself must make an effort.
Laozi's Tao and the Buddha's path mean exactly the same thing
both say a long way is walked step by step; Laozi's Tao is the nameless way of heaven and earth, the Buddha's a path to the end of dukkha.

games.q: a friend says, 'if the Buddha was a real teacher, everyone he taught would have reached nibbana.' what does the accountant's question say back?
o: a guide can give exact directions; arriving still takes the walker's steps.
everyone he taught did arrive; the sutta just doesn't list them.
he kept the last turn hidden, so only the best students would find it.
games.why: the Buddha said plainly: some do, some don't. he shows the way, like directions to Rajagaha; the walking is each person's.

practice: Sit for most of the time, nothing to fix, nowhere to get to. In the last moments, turn toward a window or a door and look out, as far as you can see. That's the view from five years of mornings, and the road keeps going past it.

wordCard.voice: The summit: five years of mornings, and the view from the top. The Buddha showed the way. The steps were yours.

orig.note: Pali, Dhammapada 276: the Tathagatas only tell the way.

carryVoice: Take this one down the mountain: you walked it. He pointed; the walking was yours. Fourteen of fourteen, and the path goes on.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 107 (Ganakamoggallana Sutta: the road to Rajagaha; the Tathagata only shows the way)

sources.q: You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers.
the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching, chapter 1 (the Tao that can be named is not the enduring Tao)
